question: Which ground aid does an aircraft's ADF work with?

options.text: A VHF direction-finding station
A VHF omni-directional range (VOR)
A distance measuring equipment (DME)
A non-directional beacon (NDB)

explanation: The ADF is the airborne receiver; the NDB is the simple LF/MF ground transmitter it points to. Together they give en route bearings and non-precision approaches.

question: How does an NDB radiate its signal?

options.text: Vertically polarized, in two lobes along the runway
Horizontally polarized, in a narrow rotating beam
Vertically polarized, equally in all directions
Circularly polarized, straight upwards only

explanation: "Non-directional" means the beacon radiates the same signal in every direction. Its LF/MF surface wave is vertically polarized, since horizontal polarization would die out quickly.

question: What does the ADF measure?

options.text: The bearing of the NDB relative to the aircraft's fore-aft axis
The aircraft's distance from the NDB
The true bearing of the NDB from magnetic north
The magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the NDB

explanation: The ADF finds the direction of the beacon relative to the nose — a relative bearing. Heading must be added to get a magnetic bearing.

question: What is the "cone of silence" over an NDB?

options.text: A zone beyond the DOC where the ident is not heard
A zone overhead with no usable signal, widening with height
A zone overhead with no signal, narrowing with height
A zone around the NDB where only the sky wave is received

explanation: Directly over the beacon the aircraft receives no usable directional signal. The cone's diameter increases the higher the aircraft is.

question: Although NDBs were expected to be phased out, why are they still important?

options.text: They are required for all oceanic flights
At some aerodromes they provide the only instrument approach
They are more accurate than VOR at long range
They are the only aid that works above FL 300

explanation: Many aerodromes still have NDB approach procedures, and at some it is the only instrument approach available.

question: When does a loop aerial produce no output?

options.text: When the signal is vertically polarized
When the NDB uses N0NA2A emission
When it is at right angles to the incoming wave
When it is in line with the incoming wave

explanation: In line with the wave, the two vertical sides of the loop are at different phases and a voltage is produced. At right angles, both sides receive the wave in phase, the voltages cancel and there is a null.

question: What is the problem with using a loop aerial alone to find a beacon's direction?

options.text: Its two nulls give a 180° ambiguity
It works only with horizontally polarized signals
It has no null, so no direction can be found
It gives the distance, but not the direction

explanation: The loop's figure-of-eight pattern has two nulls 180° apart, so it shows the line on which the beacon lies but not which end. An automatic system cannot resolve this on its own.

question: What is the purpose of the sense aerial in an ADF?

options.text: To measure the distance to the beacon
To reduce night effect on the loop aerial
To receive the beacon's Morse identification
To resolve the 180° ambiguity of the loop

explanation: A simple aerial with a circular polar diagram is combined with the loop's figure-of-eight to give a cardioid with only one null, showing which of the loop's two nulls is correct.

question: What polar diagram results from combining the loop and sense aerial signals?

options.text: A narrow beam with side lobes
A figure-of-eight with two nulls
A cardioid with one null
A circle with no nulls

explanation: Adding the sense aerial's circle to the loop's figure-of-eight produces a heart-shaped cardioid with a single, rather ill-defined null.

question: Why is a single cardioid null not used directly for the bearing?

options.text: It points 90° away from the beacon
It is too poorly defined to meet the ±5° requirement
It appears only when the BFO is on
It disappears completely at night

explanation: The cardioid's null is broad. It is used only to choose the correct loop null; to get the needed accuracy the system switches between two cardioids.

question: How does a modern ADF sharpen the null to meet the ±5° accuracy requirement?

options.text: By selecting the BFO to give a tone
By adding a second sense aerial on the tail
By rotating the loop aerial faster
By switching rapidly between left and right cardioids

explanation: The sense aerial's polarity is reversed about 120 times a second, switching between a left-hand and a right-hand cardioid. Comparing them pins the null down precisely.

question: Roughly how often does an ADF switch between its two cardioids?

options.text: About 120 times per second
About 1 020 times per second
About 30 times per second
About 9 960 times per second

explanation: The sense aerial polarity is switched at about 120 Hz. (1 020 Hz is a typical identification tone, and 9 960 Hz is a VOR subcarrier.)

question: How is the ADF loop arranged in a modern aircraft?

options.text: A single loop rotated by a motor outside the fuselage
Fixed, with crossed elements feeding a goniometer
A loop that the pilot turns by hand to find the null
Two loops on the wing tips compared in phase

explanation: A rotating external loop is impractical, so a fixed loop with elements along and across the fuselage feeds a goniometer. A search coil inside it, with the sense signal, finds the unambiguous direction.

question: What frequency band is allocated to NDBs?

options.text: 30 to 300 kHz only
190 to 1 750 kHz
2 to 30 MHz

explanation: NDBs use 190–1 750 kHz in the LF and MF bands. Because they rely on surface wave, most are between about 250 and 450 kHz.

question: Between which frequencies are most NDBs found, and why?

options.text: About 1 000–1 750 kHz, to avoid sky-wave interference
About 500–1 000 kHz, to reduce static
About 190–200 kHz, to avoid broadcast stations
About 250–450 kHz, because they use surface wave

explanation: Surface wave range is better at lower frequencies, so most beacons cluster around 250–450 kHz.

question: What is a Locator (L)?

options.text: A low-powered NDB used for approaches, range about 10–25 NM
A high-powered en route NDB with a range over 100 NM
An NDB that transmits only during the hours of darkness
A VHF marker on the extended runway centre line

explanation: Locators serve aerodrome approaches and often supplement the ILS outer and middle markers. They may operate only during the aerodrome's published hours.

question: What range does an en route NDB typically have?

options.text: 10 to 25 NM
50 NM or more
Less than 10 NM
Exactly line of sight

explanation: En route NDBs have ranges of 50 NM or more, and some serving oceanic areas reach several hundred miles. They are used for homing, holding and airway navigation.

question: Which items make up the aircraft's ADF installation?

options.text: Loop aerial, sense aerial, control unit, receiver, display
Sense aerial, VHF radio, receiver, flight director
Loop aerial, sense aerial, transponder, display
Loop aerial, DME interrogator, receiver, display

explanation: The ADF consists of the loop and sense aerials, a control unit for tuning, the receiver and an indicator (RBI or RMI).

question: Why does an ADF have a beat frequency oscillator (BFO)?

options.text: To improve the bearing accuracy at night
To switch between the two cardioids
To reduce interference from thunderstorms
To make an unmodulated carrier audible as a tone

explanation: An unmodulated carrier (the N0N part) cannot be heard on a normal receiver. The BFO mixes in an offset frequency to produce an audible tone of, say, 400 or 1 020 Hz.

question: For an N0NA1A beacon, how should the BFO be used?

options.text: On for tuning only, off for identification and monitoring
Off at all times
On for tuning, identification and monitoring
Off for tuning, on for identification only

explanation: A1A identifies by keying an unmodulated carrier on and off, which is silent without the BFO. So the BFO must be on throughout.

question: For an N0NA2A beacon, how should the BFO be used?

options.text: Off at all times, even for tuning
Off for tuning, on for identification and monitoring
On for tuning, identification and monitoring
On for tuning, off for identification and monitoring

explanation: The carrier itself is unmodulated, so the BFO helps with tuning. The A2A ident is an amplitude-modulated tone, audible with the BFO off.

question: What does the A1A part of an NDB emission mean?

options.text: Speech sent by amplitude modulation
An unmodulated carrier with no identification
Morse sent by interrupting an unmodulated carrier
Morse sent as an amplitude-modulated tone

explanation: A1A is telegraphy by keying the carrier on and off. A2A sends the Morse as a modulated audio tone that any AM receiver can hear.

question: How many letters does an NDB identification normally have?

options.text: Exactly three
Two or three
Four or five
One

explanation: NDBs identify with a 2- or 3-letter Morse code.

question: Which type of NDB emission gives the greater range?

options.text: N0NA1A
N0NA2A
Both give exactly the same range
A3E

explanation: N0NA1A beacons achieve longer ranges than N0NA2A, although N0NA2A is recommended internationally for long-range beacons.

question: What does an ADF needle on an RBI show?

options.text: The true bearing of the NDB
The QDR of the aircraft from the NDB
The magnetic bearing of the NDB
The relative bearing of the NDB

explanation: On a basic RBI the scale's 000 is fixed to the aircraft's nose, so the needle shows relative bearing. Some RBIs let heading be set manually to read magnetic bearing.

question: What does the head of an RMI needle tuned to an NDB show?

options.text: The relative bearing of the NDB
The true bearing from the NDB
The magnetic bearing to the NDB (QDM)
The magnetic bearing from the NDB (QDR)

explanation: The ADF still supplies relative bearing, but the RMI card is driven by magnetic heading, so the needle reads the QDM. Its tail reads the QDR.

question: An aircraft heading 300°M has a relative bearing of 136° to an NDB. What is the magnetic bearing of the NDB?
explanation: MB = MH + RB = 300° + 136° = 436°, minus 360° = 076°. Subtracting instead gives 164°.

question: An aircraft heading 045°M has an NDB at relative bearing 270°. What is the QDM to the NDB?
explanation: QDM = MH + RB = 045° + 270° = 315°. The aircraft is on the 135° QDR from the beacon.

question: An aircraft heading 210°M has an NDB at relative bearing 060°. On which QDR from the NDB is the aircraft?
explanation: QDM = 210° + 060° = 270°, so the QDR (the reciprocal) is 090°.

question: An RMI tuned to an NDB shows the needle head on 250°. The aircraft is heading 280°M. What is the relative bearing of the NDB?
explanation: RB = MB − MH = 250° − 280° = −30° → 330°. The beacon is 30° left of the nose.

question: How can some RBIs be made to show the magnetic bearing of an NDB?

options.text: By manually setting the heading on the rotatable card
By selecting the sense aerial only
By tuning a VOR at the same time
By switching the BFO on

explanation: On some RBIs the pilot can rotate the compass card to the current heading; the needle then reads magnetic bearing, but the card must be reset whenever heading changes.

question: With an RMI, ADF bearings are referenced to magnetic north where?

options.text: At the aerodrome reference point
At the NDB
At the nearest VOR
At the aircraft

explanation: The ADF measures relative bearing at the aircraft, and the RMI adds the aircraft's magnetic heading, so the bearing uses the aircraft's meridian and variation. A VOR bearing uses the station's.

question: Which is a use of an NDB?

options.text: Holding in a race-track pattern overhead
Giving the aircraft's ground speed
Measuring the aircraft's distance to touchdown
Providing glide path guidance to the runway

explanation: NDBs give en route bearings, homing and tracking along airways, holding patterns and runway approach procedures. They give no distance or vertical guidance.

question: When ADF bearings are plotted, where is variation applied to get a true bearing?

options.text: At the NDB, because it is the fixed point
Halfway between the aircraft and the NDB
Variation is never applied to ADF bearings
At the aircraft, because the bearing is measured there

explanation: The ADF measures direction at the aircraft, relative to the aircraft's heading, so the aircraft's variation is used. Convergency between the aircraft's and the beacon's meridians must also be allowed for.

question: A pilot homes to an NDB by keeping the relative bearing at 000° in a crosswind. What track will result?

options.text: A spiral that never reaches the NDB
A curved track, ending into wind
A straight track to the NDB
A track that misses the NDB downwind

explanation: Keeping the beacon on the nose without allowing for drift makes the aircraft turn steadily into wind, giving a curved path that arrives at the beacon heading into wind.

question: An aircraft must track 080° inbound to an NDB with 20° starboard drift. What heading and relative bearing will hold the track?

options.text: Heading 060°, relative bearing 340°
Heading 100°, relative bearing 340°
Heading 060°, relative bearing 020°
Heading 100°, relative bearing 020°

explanation: Starboard drift is subtracted: heading = 080° − 20° = 060°. The beacon then lies 20° right of the nose: RB 020°.

question: An aircraft must track 080° inbound to an NDB with 28° port drift. What heading and relative bearing will hold the track?

options.text: Heading 108°, relative bearing 332°
Heading 052°, relative bearing 028°
Heading 052°, relative bearing 332°
Heading 108°, relative bearing 028°

explanation: Port drift is added: heading = 080° + 28° = 108°. The beacon then lies 28° left of the nose: RB 332°.

question: An aircraft must track 100° outbound from an NDB with 23° starboard drift. What heading and relative bearing will hold the track?

options.text: Heading 077°, relative bearing 157°
Heading 123°, relative bearing 157°
Heading 123°, relative bearing 203°
Heading 077°, relative bearing 203°

explanation: Starboard drift is subtracted: heading 077°. Outbound, the beacon is behind; the tail of the track (280°) is 203° relative to a heading of 077°.

question: An aircraft must track 090° outbound from an NDB with 20° port drift. What heading and relative bearing will hold the track?

options.text: Heading 070°, relative bearing 160°
Heading 110°, relative bearing 160°
Heading 110°, relative bearing 200°
Heading 070°, relative bearing 200°

explanation: Port drift is added: heading 110°. The beacon lies on 270° magnetic from the aircraft, which is 270° − 110° = 160° relative.

question: Flying inbound on a steady heading with the NDB initially dead ahead, the relative bearing slowly increases. What drift is the aircraft experiencing?

options.text: Starboard drift
Drift cannot be found from this
Port drift
No drift

explanation: The wind is pushing the aircraft left of track, so the beacon moves right of the nose and the relative bearing increases. The pilot turns right to regain track, then applies an estimated drift.

question: Inbound to an NDB, a pilot turns 30° right to regain track after port drift. What relative bearing shows that track has been regained?
explanation: With the heading 30° right of the track, the beacon will be 30° left of the nose when back on track: relative bearing 330°.

question: Inbound to an NDB, a pilot has allowed 10° for port drift and is on track. What relative bearing should be held?
explanation: With 10° port drift the heading is 10° right of track, so the beacon sits 10° left of the nose at RB 350°. If the drift estimate is correct this stays constant to the beacon.

question: Outbound from an NDB on a steady heading equal to the track, the relative bearing reads 190°. What drift is there?

options.text: 10° starboard drift
190° of drift
10° port drift
No drift

explanation: With no drift the beacon would be at 180°. Drifting right of track puts the beacon further left of the tail, so RB increases to 190°: 10° starboard drift. Port drift would show 170°.

question: How is the vertical separation between aircraft in an NDB holding stack normally arranged?

options.text: At least 500 ft between levels
At least 1 000 ft between levels
At least 2 000 ft between levels
Separation is by time, not height

explanation: Aircraft in the stack are separated vertically by at least 1 000 ft and move down a level as the one below becomes free.

question: In which situations does a pilot need to maintain a track using the ADF?

options.text: Only when homing to the NDB with no wind
Only in the hold, never on airways
On airways, in holds, on NDB let-downs and when intercepting
Only when ATC provides radar vectors

explanation: Track maintenance is needed along airway centre lines between NDBs, in holds over an NDB or locator, on NDB let-downs and when ATC asks the aircraft to intercept and hold a track.

question: Outbound from an NDB, the pilot has turned 30° to regain track after 10° port drift. What relative bearing shows the aircraft is back on track?
explanation: Port drift has carried the aircraft left of track, so it turns 30° right. Back on track the beacon lies on the reciprocal of the track, which is now 150° relative (for example track 090°, heading 120°, beacon on 270°: 270 − 120 = 150°).

question: On what is an NDB's designated operational coverage (DOC) based?

options.text: The NDB's line-of-sight range
The NDB's sky-wave skip distance
A night-time signal-to-noise protection ratio of 3:1
A daytime signal-to-noise protection ratio of 3:1

explanation: The DOC is the range within which, by day, the wanted signal is at least three times the unwanted one, giving the required bearing accuracy. Beyond it, and at night, errors increase.

question: How does precipitation static show on the ADF?

options.text: A loss of the ident with a steady needle
A wandering needle and a background hiss
The needle locked at 180° relative
The needle swinging rapidly to point at a storm

explanation: Water and ice particles striking the airframe build up static, lowering the signal-to-noise ratio. The needle wanders and a hiss is heard, sometimes on VHF too.

question: What effect do thunderstorms have on an ADF?

options.text: The needle may point towards the active cell
Only the audio is affected; the needle is unaffected
The needle always points 180° away from the storm
The ADF works more accurately due to stronger signals

explanation: Lightning is a powerful wide-band static source, including LF and MF. The needle can swing to the Cb with each discharge and, with several cells, may point at them for long periods.

question: What causes ADF night effect?

options.text: Increased coastal refraction at night
The loss of the surface wave over land at night
Sky waves arriving with the surface wave after the D-layer disappears
The NDB reducing its power after sunset

explanation: With the D-layer gone at night, E-layer sky waves return at fairly short ranges. They interfere in phase with the surface wave and induce currents in the loop's horizontal members.

question: At about what range from an NDB does night effect become significant?

options.text: Only beyond 1 000 NM
About 70–100 NM
About 300–400 NM
About 10–20 NM

explanation: Night effect first becomes significant at roughly 70–100 NM, where the first sky waves come down and mix with the surface wave.

question: When is ADF night effect at its worst?

options.text: On winter afternoons
At midnight
At midday
Around dawn and dusk

explanation: The ionosphere is in transition around sunrise and sunset, so sky-wave contamination is most erratic then.

question: How does night effect show on the ADF?

options.text: A loud crackle each few seconds
The ident changing to another station
A steady needle pointing 180° out
Fading audio and a hunting needle

explanation: The mixing of sky and surface waves makes the signal fade and the needle hunt back and forth.

question: How is night effect reduced by aerial design?

options.text: A longer sense aerial mounted on the tail fin
Short vertical elements and screening above and below
A horizontally polarized loop aerial
Switching between the cardioids more slowly

explanation: Keeping the loop's vertical elements short and screening the aerial from above and below reduces pick-up of the sky wave, but does not eliminate it.

question: Which is good practice when using an ADF at night?

options.text: Avoid using it within 1 hour of sunrise or sunset
Use the NDB only beyond its published range
Fly lower to stay below the sky wave
Turn the BFO off to stop sky-wave interference

explanation: At night: identify positively and keep checking, avoid the hour around sunrise and sunset, stay within the (daytime) promulgated range, treat a wandering needle with caution and cross-check with other aids.

question: Why should an NDB always be positively identified at night, even within its DOC?

options.text: The NDB changes frequency at night
The NDB turns off its identification at night
Sky waves from distant co-channel stations may interfere
The D-layer reflects the NDB's own signal back

explanation: The LF/MF bands are crowded. By day the DOC protects against stations on the same frequency, but at night their sky waves can arrive from far beyond their daytime range.

question: What causes mountain effect, and how is it reduced?

options.text: Heavier precipitation over hills; fly lower
Reflection and diffraction by high ground; fly higher
Sky waves reflected from peaks; use the BFO
Magnetic anomalies in rock; use true bearings

explanation: Mountains reflect and diffract the radio waves, causing bearing errors that are worse at low level. Climbing reduces them.

question: Why does coastal refraction occur?

options.text: The ionosphere is lower over the sea
Sea spray reverses the polarization
The surface wave slows down over the sea
The surface wave speeds up over the sea

explanation: Less energy is absorbed over water, so the part of the wave front over the sea travels faster and the wave bends towards the coast.

question: An aircraft over the sea uses an inland NDB whose signal crosses the coast at a shallow angle. How will coastal refraction affect its fix?

options.text: The fix will be further from the coast than it really is
The fix will be correct; only the range is affected
The fix will be closer to the coast than it really is
The fix will be displaced along the coastline only

explanation: The wave bends towards the coast as it passes onto the sea, so the bearing makes the aircraft appear closer to the coast than it is.

question: At what angle to the coastline is coastal refraction least?

options.text: 0° (parallel)

explanation: Refraction is negligible when the signal crosses the coast at right angles and increases as the crossing angle becomes shallower.

question: Which helps reduce coastal refraction error?

options.text: Flying lower over the sea
Using signals parallel to the coast
Using an NDB on or near the coast
Using an NDB well inland

explanation: Use beacons on or near the coast, fly higher, and choose signals that cross the coast at or near 90°.

question: What causes quadrantal error in an ADF?

options.text: The airframe bending signals towards its fore-aft axis
The NDB's signal splitting into four lobes
Sky waves arriving from four directions at night
The aircraft's compass being misaligned in four quadrants

explanation: The airframe has a strong electrical field along its fore-aft axis, which refracts incoming signals towards that axis and distorts the loop's reception pattern.

question: On which relative bearings is quadrantal error greatest?
explanation: The error is greatest in the quadrants, midway between the aircraft's axes. Modern equipment has manufacturer's corrections built in; older systems were "swung" to measure it.

question: What causes ADF dip (bank angle) error?

options.text: Turning changes the sky wave's angle of arrival
The compass dips during turns and misleads the RMI
Banking moves the NDB into the cone of silence
Bank lets currents form in the loop's horizontal members

explanation: The loop is designed for vertically polarized waves. When banked, horizontal components induce currents in the top and bottom of the loop, blurring the nulls. The error disappears in level flight.

question: Why must an ADF be continuously monitored when used for an approach?

options.text: Most ADF indicators have no failure warning
The NDB switches off at the decision height
The needle always lags the true bearing by 5°
ADF bearings are valid only for 30 seconds

explanation: A failure is not readily obvious, because most ADF indicators have no warning flag. The ident must be monitored and other aids cross-checked.

question: Which way does the ADF needle move when an active Cb discharges nearby?

options.text: It freezes on its last bearing
It swings rapidly towards the storm
It rotates continuously
It swings rapidly away from the storm

explanation: A lightning discharge is a strong burst of LF/MF energy, so the needle points briefly at it. During Cb activity the ADF may be better at showing where the cells are than where the beacon is.

question: What is the protection ratio on which an NDB's DOC is based?
explanation: Within the DOC, by day, the wanted signal must be at least three times the unwanted signal.

question: An NDB's range is to be doubled. By how much must its power be increased?

options.text: Sixteen times
Eight times
Twice
Four times

explanation: Range is proportional to the square root of power, so doubling range needs four times the power.

question: An NDB transmits 400 W. What is its approximate range over water?

options.text: 20 NM
60 NM
40 NM

explanation: Over water, range ≈ 3√P = 3 × √400 = 3 × 20 = 60 NM. Over land it would be about 2 × 20 = 40 NM.

question: An NDB has a range of 30 NM over land. What is its power output?
explanation: Over land, 2√P = 30, so √P = 15 and P = 225 W. Using the sea factor of 3 instead gives 100 W.

question: How do frequency and precipitation affect NDB range?

options.text: Lower frequency reduces range; precipitation has no effect
Higher frequency increases range; precipitation increases it
Lower frequency increases range; precipitation reduces it
Frequency has no effect; precipitation increases range

explanation: Lower frequencies give a stronger surface wave (more diffraction, less attenuation). All precipitation, including snow, reduces range and accuracy.

question: What accuracy is expected from ADF?

options.text: ±5° within the DOC, by day only
±5° at any range, day and night
±10° within the DOC, by day only
±2° within the DOC, day and night

explanation: The accepted accuracy is ±5° within the designated operational coverage by day. This is the bearing accuracy only and excludes compass error.
